desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list is passed to your function as an array holding the node values from head to tail; an empty array is an empty list. You may build real nodes from it first, or work on the array directly. The result is also returned as an array of values from head to tail.

Cut the list into exactly k consecutive parts, in the original order, so that the sizes of any two parts differ by at most 1 and the parts that come earlier are never smaller than the parts that come later. When the list has fewer than k nodes, the last parts are empty.

Return the parts as an array of k arrays, each holding the values of one part from head to tail (an empty part is []). For example, [1,2,3] with k = 5 gives [[1],[2],[3],[],[]] and ten nodes with k = 3 give sizes 4, 3, 3.
hints: First decide how large each part must be. With n nodes and k parts, every part gets at least n // k nodes.
The n mod k leftover nodes go one each to the first n mod k parts, so those parts have n // k + 1 nodes.

Count the length, then walk the list once: for part i take n // k + (1 if i < n % k else 0) nodes, detach them by setting the next of the last taken node to null, and continue from the following node. Parts beyond the end of the list stay empty.
editorial: The size rule is forced: the sizes must be as equal as possible and non-increasing, so the first n mod k parts have n // k + 1 nodes and the remaining parts have n // k.

First count the nodes. Then for each part walk size - 1 steps from the part's first node to its last node, remember the node after it, cut the link, and start the next part there. Each node is visited a constant number of times, so the time is O(n + k); apart from the output, no extra space is needed.
